summary: Defines the IMAP UIDONLY extension. Once enabled, the server reports mailbox changes using only Unique Identifiers (UIDs), not message numbers, and clients cannot use message numbers in requests. This saves clients and servers the effort of mapping between the two. The status is experimental.

eli5.summary: Each email has a seat number that can change and a permanent ID. This tells email programs to use only the permanent ID to avoid mix-ups.

subtitle: An IMAP extension that drops message sequence numbers entirely, so clients and servers talk only in permanent UIDs.

tldr.problem: IMAP lets clients refer to messages by sequence number or by UID. Keeping a map between the two costs clients and servers resources.
tldr.mechanism: A client turns on the UIDONLY extension with ENABLE. From then on, commands must use UIDs, and the server announces changes with UIDFETCH and VANISHED responses that carry UIDs only.
tldr.outcome: This is an Experimental extension that works with IMAP4rev1 and IMAP4rev2. Using message numbers once it is enabled draws a tagged BAD response with the UIDREQUIRED code.

today: RFC 9586 is an Experimental IMAP extension published in May 2024, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 9051 and RFC 3501.

sections.title: Why Drop Message Numbers
sections.content:
RFC 9586 defines the UIDONLY extension to the Internet Message Access Protocol. It lets clients ask servers to use and return only Unique Identifiers (UIDs) and no message sequence numbers. This helps both sides reduce the resources needed to keep a map between message numbers and UIDs.

The extension is compatible with both IMAP4rev1 (RFC 3501) and IMAP4rev2 (RFC 9051). A server advertises it by including the UIDONLY capability.
sections.eli5: Email programs can name a message by its current place in line or by a permanent ID. Keeping both lists in sync is chore work, so this lets them use just the ID.

sections.title: Turning It On
sections.content:
Because UIDONLY changes how unsolicited responses about new, expunged or changed messages look, the client must first enable it with the ENABLE command. The server confirms with an ENABLED response.

Once it is enabled, the client MUST NOT use message sequence numbers (including the special marker, an asterisk) in any command arguments. The server MUST answer such a command with a tagged BAD response that includes the UIDREQUIRED response code. The server MUST NOT return message sequence numbers in any response.
sections.eli5: The mail program has to ask 'can we use only IDs from now on?' and the server says yes. After that, using the old seat numbers gets a polite refusal.

sections.title: What Changes in Commands and Responses
sections.content:
With UIDONLY enabled, the plain FETCH, STORE, SEARCH, COPY and MOVE commands are prohibited and MUST get a tagged BAD. Clients use the UID versions instead. In UID SEARCH, the plain sequence-set criterion is prohibited; clients use ALL or UID <sequence set>.

Responses change too. Fetch data that would come as FETCH responses is sent as UIDFETCH responses, which start with the UID. This includes flag changes that the server announces on its own. Expunged messages are announced with VANISHED responses (defined in RFC 7162) instead of EXPUNGE. The extension does not affect EXISTS or RECENT responses.

UID MOVE and UID COPY SHOULD return the COPYUID response code from RFC 4315. A server that advertises UIDONLY MUST NOT return UIDNOTSTICKY.
sections.eli5: The mail program must now say 'give me message ID 25900', never 'give me the fifth one'. And the server answers by ID too, including when messages are deleted.

sections.title: Other Extensions and Rejected Design
sections.content:
CONDSTORE is compatible: the MODSEQ data item moves into UIDFETCH responses. QRESYNC is compatible too, but the fourth SELECT QRESYNC parameter (message sequence match data) MUST NOT be used, and the server MUST answer with a tagged BAD if it sees one. A server need not implement CONDSTORE or QRESYNC to support UIDONLY.

Any other extension command that takes sequence numbers MUST be rejected with a tagged BAD. For example, SORT and THREAD are prohibited, but UID SORT and UID THREAD can be used.

An earlier draft proposed sending FETCH responses with the message number always set to 0. That was considered too risky, because it could cause unexpected side effects and cache corruption in client code that was not updated to handle missing message numbers.
sections.eli5: Other mail features keep working as long as they also use IDs. The designers once tried sending a fake seat number of zero, but decided that would confuse programs that were not ready for it.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The extension is not believed to add any security considerations beyond those that already apply to IMAP4rev1 and IMAP4rev2.

IANA added the UIDONLY capability to the IMAP Capabilities registry and the UIDREQUIRED response code to the IMAP Response Codes registry, both with RFC 9586 as the reference.
sections.eli5: It does not make mail any more or less risky than before. The new names were just written in the official lists.
